newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Barney's would be challenge for Dickson.
newsitem.headline: Barney's would be challenge for Dickson.

text.p: Dickson Concepts (Int'l) Ltd has a proven record of turning around troubled retailers but the Hong Kong firm could face a considerable challenge if it takes on beleaguered U.S. luxury store Barney's Inc, analysts said.
"Barney's is in a different retail market, the U.S. market, which they may not be very familiar with. Other Asian retailers in the U.S. are not doing well," said Stephanie Wang at James Capel.
"It's really, really competitive. It's hard to tell how many years it will take for Barney's to make a profit."
Dickson Concepts said in July it was mulling a bid for the privately-held luxury clothing store but since then has kept silent on its interest in Barney's, which has filed for bankruptcy.
Newspapers reported this month Dickson had made an initial offer to buy Barney's for a sum possibly between US$300 million and US$400 million. Both companies declined to comment.
Dickson is led by 40-year-old entrepreneur and socialite Dickson Poon, who started off as a sales assistant in one of his father's watch and jewellery shops.
He launched his own business in this field in 1980, before taking over a listed real estate investment and development firm in 1986 and building it into a prominent luxury retailer.
Dickson's latest feat was the turnaround of luxury London department store Harvey Nichols.

In 1991, Dickson paid 51 million sterling for the loss-making store. In June this year, Harvey Nichols reported a 53 percent surge in pretax profits for the year to March 30 to 9.2 million sterling (US$14.5 million).
"Barney's acquisition would be much bigger than Nichols," said Wang.

Financing the acquisition of the loss-making U.S. retailer, investing in inventory and possibly taking on debts or court costs due to litigation between Barney's and Japanese retailer Isetan Co Ltd, could affect Dickson's earnings and stock performance in the short term, analysts said.
"Initially there might be a little negative impact on stock price for a very short period, only because if it really went ahead it would be a very big acquisition," Wang said.

"To acquire such a big firm might dilute Dickson's earnings," she said. "To acquire a money-losing firm, time is needed to turn it around...as Dickson's usual strategy is to take a controlling stake, so it would consolidate (Barney's) losses initially."

However, an analyst at OCBC Securities said cash-rich Dickson's should be able to absorb such a deal without too much strain on its profit. It would also represent a good strategic move for the Hong Kong firm in the long run.
"Barney isn't really generating a lot of profit now," she said. "I have confidence Dickson will be able to achieve that and that Barney will contribute to Dickson's longer-term growth."
Some analysts believed Dickson could repeat on Barney's the magic it worked on Harvey Nichols. "If they bought it...I'm sure they would do to it what they did to Harvey Nichols," one said.
Analysts agreed the impact of the Barney's deal would depend ultimately on the final terms.
"It could be good and it might be bad. it depends on the deal and the aspects of the deal," said Tara Osborough, retail analyst at Asia Equity.
But some believed Dickson was unlikely to make any bid for loss-making Barney's at all, given that it would be difficult for the potential buyer to secure favourable terms.
